notes.urn:cts:greekLit:tlg2200.tlg00521.opp-gr: The printed page's list of manuscript sigla, which intrudes into the Greek of 1.3, has been left out, as have the edition's section numbers and page marks where they could be identified. Several readings are emended from evident scanning errors: ἄξοι in 1.1 is taken as ἀξιοῖ ('asks'), a reading that supplies the subject Demosthenes; ἴφθη as ἔφθη; <Ἀιξμσὸπο> as Ἀθηναῖοι; ἰδέων as ἰδίων. In 12.2 the sentence beginning 'if the deed were going to be the people's' is grammatically incomplete: ὑμεῖς has no verb, so something may be lost, or the construction may break off. The conditional is resumed in the next stretch ('I would have spoken such words'), and the extent of the imagined speech is uncertain. The opening of 8.2's quoted reasoning uses 'this one' (τοῦτον) for the one Athenian; the reference is clear from context. In 12.1, ἱερῶν, ὁσίων may contrast sacred with secular things rather than naming two religious items.

Section 18: 'the orator from Byzantium' is evidently Python of Byzantium, who is named in the lines that follow. Section 26: the transmitted κἂν φύγ’ ὡς ἴ’ τὸ βῆμα is garbled; translated as κἂν φύγωσι τὸ βῆμα ('even if they flee the platform'), which fits the following κρύπτωσιν. Section 25: ἵξετε read as ἕξετε, parallel to οὐχ ἕξετε. Section 21: περὶ τῆς ἀνθρωπείας τύχης is literally 'about the human fortune'; taken as the fortunes of the captives, but the sense is not certain. Section 26: ἔνα read as ἵνα.

30: "ten thousand Pythons" apparently refers to Python of Byzantium, the orator who served Philip. 34: the transmitted τῷ μίσει τι is awkward; τι is left untranslated, and the sense "in my hatred toward him" is the likely one. 35: the sentence "he does not say that he is willing to give the greater and receive the lesser" is compressed; the sense seems to be that Philip does not say so outright, though his offer implies that Demosthenes outweighs the captives. 36: the section numbered 36 is filed under the reference 35.2.

nodes.text: XXI.
After the events at Chaeronea, Philip sent [envoys], promising to return the two thousand captives if he received Demosthenes. [Demosthenes] asks to be surrendered.
Demosthenes

When the envoys arrived, men of Athens, and word spread that Philip wished to give some things to the city and to receive others from it in exchange, I immediately prepared to advise you to accept, and to welcome him as he courted the city, since it is your ancestral custom to have Macedonians grovelling before you, but certainly not to give away anything of yours, since these are not the lessons the people learned from their ancestors. But when the letter had been read out, and those who came from there had said things consistent with what was written, that you could recover the captives by handing me over to Philip, I abandoned that opinion, and I approve of both what he gives and what he asks to receive. For it would be a terrible thing if I, who for all my life have valued what benefits the city above my own safety, should now suddenly be seen to have changed.

So I rejoice with the captives, men of Athens, as they are released from Macedonian mastery | and from seeing their enemies as their masters, which seems to be the bitterest thing of all, and as they recover their fatherland and their own property and relatives and the other things they longed to enjoy. And I am fortunate, even if I seem to others the most wretched of all men: though I am depriving myself of the good things among you, and going willingly into the hands of my worst enemies, I still have sufficient consolation in being willing to suffer this while bringing some part of your affairs to a better state. For as it is sweet for them to recover their homeland, so it is sweet for me that Athens is restored to them through my life.

It was fated, it seems, men of Athens, that this whole business following the disturbance at the Pylaea, a disturbance whose instigator goes about the city beaming while everyone else grieves, should be managed for the city through me and my speeches and my decrees and my person. For when the man came with the news that Elatea had been seized, and fear made the diners rise from their tables and forced the people to assemble more quickly than the Council, no one but me dared to come forward: my goodwill, perhaps, might have been found in others too, but no one knew Philip as I did, and that is why all were silent.

And when it seemed advantageous for the Thebans to become ours, and this, men of Athens, was difficult because of those who were provoking the two cities against each other, I went there on an embassy and, as no one would ever have expected, defeated Philip's envoys in speaking before the Thebans, | and persuaded the city of Thebes to choose you, who had caused it no little pain, over Philip, who had done it many favours.

And I would not have blamed myself. For even if it was especially from that point that the hatred toward me grew in the man who now wishes to get me, still I was crowned among you, men of Athens, and those who indicted me out of envy were left with shame in their defeat. Further, when your valour had been displayed in the [battles] in which you often defeated the enemy, but the outcome did not gain the favour of fortune as well, it was through my voice that you honoured those who died nobly in the battle, for you knew that I had offered the most prayers on their behalf.

So when the burial had taken place and the funeral feast at my house, for I was honoured with this too by the relatives of the fallen, I turned at once to my concern for the captives, believing that they too were no less brave and had not come to endure this fortune through any cowardice, but that this too was no small token of their courage, that they had been captured while fighting. For the cowardly, who fear wounds, do not dare to close with the enemy, but when the battle begins they usually throw away their arms and save themselves, whereas those who resolve to accomplish something, and who bring their shields into the clash and do not spare themselves, these are the ones who are also captured.

For this reason I was considering privately how they might quickly be brought safely home, and indeed I was about to tell you how this could happen, for I found that not even Philip would be glad to have so many Athenian enemies in his own country, whom he surely would not use as soldiers, since that would be dangerous, nor could he gather them in some place and hold them there, from which it would not be easy to escape, and to keep them in chains for no purpose was neither humane nor profitable.

So it was clear that if you sent men to discuss these matters with him | and to invoke the ancient custom concerning captives, he would do what many have often done, and so would release them and send them away, wishing, besides, to have some favour stored up with you, so that, should the dispensations of the divine shift, he could remind the people of something. For he knew, he knew even now, that he had not won by virtue but had gained the advantage by fortune; and that is why I hear that he did not even crown himself, reckoning who he was and over whom he had proved superior.

While I was busy with these matters and had the speeches about them in hand, Philip's embassy forestalled my planning for them. Why did this happen in this way? That man, not expecting to get one Athenian from the Athenians, for it is enough for me to say this much, sent men to ask for this one. He does not think you so estranged from your fathers, nor has he failed to hear of the ancient wars in which, though many citizens fell into the hands of the enemy, none obtained a ransom of this kind. Rather, he reasoned to himself: "I shall ask for Demosthenes, and he will come forward and speak against it, and the people will not | give him up, and this will grieve the relatives of the captives, and the affair will take away from the orator's freedom of speech, and in this way he will have many opponents whenever he tries to say anything."

With such hopes did the excellent fellow beguile himself. But our affairs, at least, are not like that. How could they be? For when they heard the letter, none of those closest in kinship to those men, and I see many of them seated here, either shouted or clamoured that [we] must both give and receive; rather, I saw some of them weeping, for me rather than for those who had been captured. For they reasoned, I think, that their relatives' case has consolation from many precedents and has happened by the law of war, whereas mine would be something new, which had never happened before and had befallen me alone of all men. Such, men of Athens, are you: good and humane and placing the common reputation before your private interests.

And such is your part, so noble and worthy of the character of the city, and my part is perhaps no worse. I give myself up to those who have come, and I am ready to go to Macedonia, and what not one of those enriched by him has dared to say, this I both say and put in writing.

And I shall go to suffer whatever Philip decides. And of the things sweetest and most precious to all, deme, tribe, home, sacred rites, holy observances, ancestral tombs, and many others, I make little account because of my goodwill toward you. For it is, I think, both just and fitting for each side to think in this way: you to hold fast to your fellow citizens and to consider nothing so great as to require surrendering someone to the enemy, | neither gain nor fear nor the difficulty of a crisis; and each of us to shrink from nothing for what benefits you.

"But," someone says, "you are trying to persuade the people to do what is contrary both to the laws and to the way the city has lived through all time. And with what eyes shall we face the Greeks, and what fine excuse shall we give to those who ask?" Some will say such things. But as for me, if the deed were going to be the people's, and you, with me crying out and reading the laws and saying, "You are wronging, men of Athens, Solon and Draco and the rules handed down to you by your ancestors, abiding by which they went on campaign for people who were nothing to them and had no other claim on them except supplication. And why need I mention the Heraclidae or Adrastus? Why, they even manned ships to help barbarians, so that the stronger might not be free to do wrong. And I, if nothing else, am an Athenian, and I could produce for you clansmen and phratry members, and I am enrolled on the deme register, and everyone would bear me witness to these things, and to my education, and perhaps to other things bringing greater distinction than these. But for me it is enough to state my birth.

I would have spoken to you in such terms, men of Athens, if I saw you doing anything base and unworthy of the name of the city. For I, who would not let you abandon to Philip even any one of | the other Greeks, but urged you to spend both money and lives, on the ground that this post had been handed down to you by your fathers, would hardly have looked on while anyone was led off to the barbarians from your assembly, with you giving him up.

But as it is, you are clear of blame and irreproachable in every respect, and no charge of impiety will come against the people from anyone, and the whole affair will be mine, I myself giving and I myself being given up. For no decree will be recorded, "Resolved by the people of the Athenians," but "Resolved by Demosthenes concerning Demosthenes." And this means that you are in no way the worse, and that I am the same man toward you as of old.

For when I came to public affairs, I took as my models not Aeschines, nor Phrynon, that brave man who feels no shame at anything, nor Demades, nor Philocrates, but Aristides and Pericles and Nicias, men perhaps no better disposed than I toward the people, but who spoke in the more fortunate times of that day. Desiring, then, the pattern of those men's statesmanship, and distressing you in the matters in which I was benefiting you, I distressed far more the man who wanted to drive you out of affairs and to prevail himself in arms while you sat idle.

I knew, then, that this political course was not without danger, but I nevertheless thought that I ought, if it came to that, to die rather than leave the post to which I had assigned myself. Now, then, when the moment demands zeal, shall I show myself a coward? And how would that be just? I feel shame before the crowns I have had from you, men of | Athens; I feel shame before many fine speeches, many beneficial decrees; I feel shame before laws, not a few others and the one through which your navy has been preserved.

Shall I, who prevented Antiphon from burning the dockyards and handing the sea over to Philip, who showed the cleverness of the orator from Byzantium to be weaker than the just claims of the city, who hated my wicked fellow envoys and had no regard for private ties against your interests, now desert my old goodwill? And which of the Greeks do I expect to escape the notice of? For one cannot say this either, that the report of my faint-heartedness will not reach many, or that the shame will stop among these neighbors, I mean the Euboeans and Thebans and Megarians.

No, this too is a great penalty for me, that my political career has been so widely talked of. The cause is that I gave myself to the affairs of Greece, and my many embassies displayed me to the whole Greek race, and not to the Greeks alone but by now to many of the barbarians too. To the King I did not go myself, but some report of my toils is said to have reached him.

Shall I then endure that this whole earth should think the worse of me, and that some of those who envy me here among you should be able to say: "Demosthenes has destroyed the great and abundant renown that he gathered over a long time and through many labors. | That man who served as a volunteer *choregus* [sponsor of a festival chorus] and contributed triremes, who was freeing Euboea, who was rescuing the Hellespont, who was saving the Chersonese, thanks to whom men sailed from every side to crown the people, who gave himself unsparingly to every pressing need, now, when he could have made a generous gift out of his very body, was unwilling"?

"Why then," someone says, "do you not state the other ways of ransoming that you claim to have found, Demosthenes?" Because, men of Athens, though they exist, and are both honorable and customary, for I would not deny it, they require some time; and what is needed, I think, is speed. For example, if I say that money must be contributed, I shall persuade you, for no Athenian is so cruel or so unacquainted with spending for just causes that he would dare to shirk the expense. For if you came into danger on behalf of those who had wronged you and contributed eagerly, how, when the effort is for some of your own citizens, could each of you regard giving a little silver as a loss? But, you see, a decree must pass, and the collectors must go to those who owe, and the people must elect envoys to confer with Philip about the fortunes of these men. These things take five or ten days or even more, and that, I think, is hard on those who long for their own kin.

But should I state another way, which will recover the persons even against Philip's will: to summon all the Greeks? They know his greed | and that he was fond of no one, but flattered those with hopes for his own ends, and that they have been deceived and he is laughing. Should I say this, and that you must launch your triremes? There are many of them, and ready, and Chaeronea has done no damage to our affairs at sea, nor could Philip bear your ravaging his own [land], but under pressure he will give back, besides the captives, both strongholds and cities. But again, this means time, and more days than for the contributions.

But I would wish what is most pleasing to you to come about today, and no delay in this matter to occur on my account. Now, if I had as much money, men of Athens, as would ransom so many men, I would do the same as on the embassy. And what was it I did then? While the other envoys were bringing gold from there to here, I myself carried it from here to there and brought back as many of the captives as I could.

And now too I would not have hesitated to release the citizens from a worse fortune in the same way, if I had so much silver at hand. But I do not have so much. So much, do I say? Rather I have little, men of Athens, very little. For apart from my not having recovered even the smallest fraction of my inheritance, this very amount has been spent on you, and I have no base gain from any source. What is left? To contribute my life in place of money.

"What then," someone says, "if they are with us, but the man who teaches | the people what is more profitable goes away?" It is a hard thing, men of Athens, a hard thing and not without loss, but still you must bear it, setting the gain against the harm. You will not have a hardworking orator, but you will have more soldiers. You will not hear fine speeches, but you will see those who are now elsewhere. But indeed I have wronged in my words this excellent Hyperides here, most devoted to the people, and anyone else who has continued to think as I do.

From these men, then, you will demand proposals and decrees, even if they flee the speaker's platform and hide themselves and reproach you, saying: "You, men of Athens, have handed over to the Macedonians that Demosthenes who neglected his own affairs and spent his whole life in care for yours, the sleepless, the toiling, who did not take breath for even a small part of a day, who was stronger than Macedonian wealth, this man you have handed over to the Macedonians. And Philip has seen in chains the man who earlier came as an envoy. Why then do you summon us to the *barathron* [the Athenian execution pit]? Or is it so that we too may go the same way? Fine indeed are the wages of goodwill!"

If they say these things in tears, men of Athens, you will not lack a defense against them. For what I have just said to you, you will say on your own behalf: "It was not we who gave up Demosthenes, but while we were stunned and distressed and were intending to give those who had come an answer that would have made Philip more cautious, he persuaded himself that it was right for him to suffer this."

And if they rebuke you again because you left this to Demosthenes and gave way and did not prevent it or take hold of him, or repay his excessive zeal by not letting this happen, you will again have | a plausible thing to say: that you were pained when I wished to go and shouted for me to stay, but I proved stronger than the whole people. Encourage them with these words, then, and at the same time promise to be better in future, and they will believe you when you say so.

Let me then, by the trophies, by the land that we boast of having as our mother, do what I have resolved, and let no one compel me to submit to anything unworthy of my resolve. And as I go, I want to console both you and myself. For you, then, let the consolation come from my own case. For you see the reversal. Demosthenes, who poured out his flood against Philip in the assembly, will be led away from the assembly itself. And the man whom battle did not give up to the victors, this man will deliver himself into the hands of his bitterest enemy, and that enemy, having got him, will flog him, rack him, and consume his body with iron and fire.

For do not fear that I shall ever give myself over to his interests. He will perhaps be willing, scoundrel that he is, and will give land and a house and a great quantity of money, and in return for these he will expect me to go around Greece and sing a recantation: that Philip is pious, trustworthy, just, most Hellenic, and inferior to the Athenians in nothing, or not in many things. He would rather have these words come from my tongue than have ten thousand Pythons of his own. For he knows that the man who has most discredited him is the only one who could also change people's minds back.

It is likely, then, that Philip will not refrain from this attempt either, but by what I say I shall quickly draw him into anger, again calling him a plague, again a barbarian, and saying that the city of the Athenians is immortal, that the oracles concerning her cannot be proved false, and that I supposed it my duty to bring the captives safely back to her through my own person, but that she is strong even without them and knows that you have not conquered.

At this let him cut me to pieces and, if he wishes, taste my entrails. I shall bear the harshest things easily. On what reckoning? That even if I die ten thousand times now, no length of time will erase the glory I have won among the Greeks. And if this should indeed happen with any of the other Greeks, yet it will never pass out of this city; but as long as this council chamber remains, and this Pnyx, and the law courts, and the Metroon, and they will remain forever, for the gods say so, there will be some memory of what I have labored at.

And even if someone should forget the rest, how could he forget this last act at any rate? For new things are least of all blotted out by oblivion. And such, I think, is the present case: a man who is an enemy unwillingly praises me, his foe. I have also reflected that undeserved good fortune often drives men out of their senses. Philip, at any rate, does not know that in the very act of seeking to get me he becomes a witness to my goodwill toward you, and all but proclaims to everyone: "It is because of this man, you know, that I have not mastered Attica, but am still toiling and campaigning, when I could long ago have had everything."

What greater consolation, then, must I still look for? Or what crowns is this not more honorable than? For when he hates me alone so much, he also admits that I have surpassed everyone in my hatred toward him. So just as I would be ashamed if he claimed to love me, so I take pride in being hated. If I could produce my enemies among the citizens as witnesses to my better deeds, that would be a great thing, and it would be proof of the highest excellence that those who would gladly have reviled me had been compelled to praise me; so when a foreigner and an enemy does this very thing, is it not fitting that I should take pride in it and consider the letter of the man so eager to kill me a fine funeral honor?

Saying these things to myself along the road, I shall not be distressed, because Philip has admitted that I am worth more than two thousand Athenians. For he does not say that he is willing to give the greater and receive the lesser; but what I myself never yet dared to say on my own behalf before you, this the enemy teaches in other words. This, then, as I said, will bring me consolation.

36. It is time now to go, after offering this much in prayer: Apollo our ancestral god, and lady Athena, and Demeter and Kore and Iacchus, and all gods and heroes, with whom our forefathers conquered the Mede when he seemed irresistible, grant that this man may make this exchange with the city of the Athenians simply and without guile, and may bring to this business no trickery, nothing of what he is accustomed to, nothing from his own nature. And with reason, I think, I fear him, the man who has done more wrong in treaties than in arms.
